summaries.example: Imagine the sentence “A person runs.” Brito would say that the words fit together because “a person” and “runs” express ideas that can belong together. Grammar is not only about memorizing rules; it is also about how words show ways of understanding things.
summaries.summary: Radulphus Brito was a Paris master who lived around 1270–1320/21. He wrote many question-commentaries on works by Aristotle, Boethius, and Priscian. Much of his work survives in manuscripts, and some is still being edited. In grammar, Brito argued that words have ways of signifying, or showing things, and that good sentences use compatible ways of signifying. He thought these ways are connected to how people understand things and to how things are. In logic, he studied methods for gaining knowledge and logical ideas applied to ordinary concepts. He also wrote about the soul, thinking, being, universals, happiness, freedom, and virtue. His work helps us see how medieval scholars connected language, thought, reality, and action.
key_ideas: Brito was a major medieval teacher and writer in Paris.
He wrote many commentaries on Aristotle, logic, grammar, the mind, reality, and ethics.
He connected grammar with how people understand things and how things are.
He explained logic as a study of ways to gain knowledge and of logical notions.
He held that happiness chiefly involves thoughtful understanding and that reason helps guide free choice.
summaries.why_it_matters: Brito shows that people in the Middle Ages were doing detailed work on questions that still matter: How does language carry meaning? What makes an argument good? How do our minds understand the world? What makes a choice free or responsible? Studying him also shows that old philosophical texts can preserve ideas that scholars are still investigating today.

important_terms.definition: A scholar who taught at the University of Paris in the late thirteenth and early fourteenth centuries.
The study of how words and sentences are formed and fit together.
A way that a word shows or presents something in speech.
A careful way of thinking about arguments and knowledge.
A general idea, such as the idea of being a human rather than one particular human.

questions_to_think_about: How can the way we use a word show how we understand something?
Why might a good argument need rules?
Can a general idea, such as “animal,” exist outside our minds?
How might thinking carefully change a choice?

summaries.example: Consider the term “human.” In one setting it may be treated as a substance, in another as the subject of a statement, and in another as a term within a syllogism. Brito uses this kind of distinction to explain why different logical works can discuss the same word without having exactly the same subject. Logic concerns the concept under a logical description, not merely the sound of the word or the external thing.
summaries.summary: Radulphus Brito was an influential master of arts at Paris, active from roughly the 1290s until his death in 1320/21. His extensive commentaries engage the Aristotelian corpus, Boethian logic, and Priscian’s grammar, while his theological work is much less studied and often unedited. Brito’s grammar belongs to the modistic tradition. It explains grammatical construction through modes of signifying that arise from modes of understanding and ultimately from modes of being. His logic has two related presentations: it concerns methods of acquiring scientific knowledge, especially syllogistic reasoning, and it concerns second intentions, or logical qualifications applied to concepts. This framework lets him distinguish the different roles a term can have in the Categories, De interpretatione, and Analytics, and it leads him to exclude truth itself from logic. His psychology treats the animate body as the subject of the science of the soul, describes the soul as its substantial form, and explains intellectual cognition through agent and possible intellects. In metaphysics he argues that being belongs to essence, develops an account of modes of being, and gives a moderate realist account of universals. In ethics he places philosophical happiness in intellectual knowledge, explains free will through intellectual deliberation, and changes his account of moral virtue between two commentaries.
key_ideas: Brito’s philosophical corpus consists largely of question-commentaries on Aristotle, Boethius, and Priscian; many texts remain in manuscript or are only partly edited.
His grammar treats signifying speech or expression as its subject and grounds grammatical compatibility in modes of signifying derived through understanding from modes of being.
His logic can be described both as a study of methods for acquiring scientific knowledge and as a study of second intentions.
Brito argues that truth belongs to assertions because of real states of affairs, whereas logical notions explain the validity of deductions.
In psychology, the soul is the substantial form of an organic living body; intellectual cognition begins from an image but concerns an essence.
In metaphysics, Brito identifies essence and being, gives an account of different modes of being, and defends a moderate realism about universals.
summaries.why_it_matters: Brito is important because his work connects several areas usually studied separately. His account of grammar links linguistic structure with thought and ontology. His logic of second intentions offers a way to explain how one expression can be examined under different logical roles. His psychology addresses the relation of bodily images to intellectual understanding, while his metaphysics and ethics show how theories of being and cognition shape accounts of universals, happiness, freedom, and virtue. His texts also illustrate how medieval philosophy developed through commentary and debate rather than through isolated systems.

important_terms.definition: A late-thirteenth-century Parisian master whose writings link developments in thirteenth- and fourteenth-century logic and philosophy of language.
A medieval approach holding that grammatical forms reflect ways of understanding things, which in turn reflect ways things are.
The formal feature by which a part of speech presents something in a particular way.
A first concept qualified by a logical notion, such as understanding human as a species or substance.
The study of being in general, its attributes, parts, causes, and principles.
The essence or capacity that makes a living body capable of its characteristic operations.
A general essence considered as capable of being separated from matter by the intellect, or as actually known universally.
Brito’s view that intellectual judgment can deliberate about an apparent good and thereby restrain the will.

questions_to_think_about: Does a theory of grammar need to say something about reality, or can grammar be purely formal?
Why might the same term be studied differently in several logical treatises?
What is gained by distinguishing the truth of a premise from the validity of an inference?
If the will desires what appears good, how can deliberation preserve freedom?
In what sense can a universal exist independently of the intellect, and in what sense can it not?

summaries.example: Suppose a student says, “A dog is running.” Brito would ask not only whether the sentence sounds correct, but also whether the ways its parts signify fit together. “A dog” presents a qualified substance, while “is running” presents an action being performed. The sentence works because these meanings are compatible. For Brito, grammatical order is connected to how people understand things and to the kinds of things they are.
summaries.summary: Radulphus Brito was a scholar at the University of Paris who lived around 1270–1320/21. He wrote question-commentaries on much of Aristotle’s philosophy, on Boethian logic, and on Priscian’s grammar. Many writings survive only in manuscripts, so scholars are still editing and interpreting them. Brito’s grammar belongs to the modistic tradition, which explains grammatical forms through modes of signifying. These modes are connected to modes of understanding, which are in turn connected to modes of being. A phrase is grammatical when the modes of signifying of its parts are compatible. Brito’s logic studies both the methods used to gain scientific knowledge and second intentions: concepts considered under logical descriptions such as substance, subject, species, or syllogistic term. This helps him explain why different logical books can discuss the same word in different ways. He separates the truth of an assertion from the validity of a deduction. In psychology, Brito describes the soul as the substantial form of an organic living body. Sensory powers use bodily organs, while the intellectual power does not, although thinking begins from sensory images. In metaphysics he argues that essence and being are identical, distinguishes different modes of being, and gives a moderate realist account of universals. In ethics he presents philosophical happiness as intellectual knowledge, explains free choice through deliberation, and gives different accounts of moral virtue in two commentaries.
key_ideas: Brito was a productive Parisian scholar whose works comment on many ancient and medieval texts.
He treated grammar as a theoretical discipline with practical use, grounded in how words signify.
He offered two ways to describe logic: as a science of knowledge-making methods and as a science of second intentions.
His account of the soul focuses on the living, organized body rather than treating the soul as unrelated to the body.
He held that intellectual thought begins with sensory images but reaches the essence of a thing.
His ethical views emphasize contemplation, intellectual judgment, and a changing account of where moral virtues reside.
summaries.why_it_matters: Brito’s philosophy shows how language, mind, reality, and conduct can be studied as connected questions. His work gives a detailed example of medieval reasoning about meaning: words are not just sounds, and logical terms are not simply the same as physical objects. His discussions also help explain how medieval thinkers used Aristotle while disagreeing with one another and sometimes revising their own positions.

important_terms.definition: A medieval master at the University of Paris who wrote extensively on language, logic, psychology, metaphysics, and ethics.
A medieval theory that grammar reflects ways of signifying, understanding, and being.
The way a word presents something in speech, such as as a substance, action, or quality.
A logical concept formed when an ordinary concept is considered under a logical description.
The part of philosophy concerned with being, its features, and its causes.
The form or actuality that makes a living body a particular kind of living thing.
A general concept or essence, such as human or animal, that can apply to many individuals.

questions_to_think_about: Should grammar be connected to the nature of things, or only to the rules of a language?
How is a logical notion different from an ordinary concept?
Why might Brito say that an argument can be valid even though its subject matter is not itself true?
Does a will remain free if it always wants what seems good?
What might explain Brito’s change between his two accounts of moral virtue?
